answer.answer: Five incidents are open, two in Dune Field, two in Salt Flat Field and one in Wadi Field, and they have cost about 31,830 barrels, about $2.23 million in lost revenue at an assumed $70 a barrel [1]. The high-severity ones are W-12 (Dune, shut in) [2], W-36 (Salt Flat, shut in) [3], and W-34 (Salt Flat, sand eroding its flowline) [4]. The medium ones are W-05 (Dune, pressure swings) [5] and W-25 (Wadi, pump vibration) [6].

answer.answer: W-17, a Wadi Field well, went down on 4 March 2026 when its electric pump (ESP) tripped on a motor fault, and it restarted on 18 March 2026 [1][2]. The repair found the motor's winding insulation had broken down, with light scale on the pump stages, and replaced the pump and cable [3]. Together the failure and repair lost about 17,940 barrels, about $1,256,000 in lost revenue at an assumed $70 a barrel [4][5].

answer.answer: It was not a one-off: the pump that failed in March 2026 on W-17 (Wadi Field) came from batch 7Q-0419, as did pumps that failed on W-09 (Dune Field) in October 2025 [3] and W-27 (Wadi Field) in August 2026 [2]. Each teardown found motor winding insulation breakdown [4][5][6], and the three outages together lost about 43,850 barrels, about $3.07 million in lost revenue at an assumed $70 a barrel [1]. Other pumps from batch 7Q-0419 may be at risk.

answer.answer: Water is rising steadily in Wadi Field, but it hasn't taken over. The field's average water cut (the share of water in what wells bring up) went from about 33% in January 2026 to about 44% in November [1]. Field notes attribute the rise to water flood breakthrough, and oil was still about 9,100 barrels a day in October [2].

sources.label: Shift report 23 Oct 2026
sources.quote: Water cut trend: 32.5 % in January 2026, 43.2 % over the last 30 days, 43.7 % today, so the water flood breakthrough is still pushing it up.

answer.could_not_verify: I did not check which individual wells are rising fastest.

answer.answer: The sand alarm on W-34, a Salt Flat Field well, is still open: it started on 9 November 2026 and has cost about 1,063 barrels, about $74,410 in lost revenue at an assumed $70 a barrel [1][2]. The procedure requires acknowledging the alarm, checking for noise causes, then cutting the choke (flow valve) by 2/64 in steps of 30 minutes, with sampling within 1 hour [3][4]. After the alarm clears, the choke must stay unchanged for at least 2 hours, and the Production Engineer approves return to normal rate [3][5].

sources.label: Incident note IN-067
sources.quote: The well is producing on the 24/64 choke. The incident remains **open**.

sources.label: SOP-OPS-002 response steps
sources.quote: **Acknowledge** the alarm in the control system and note the time, well and reading. Inform the Production Supervisor.

sources.label: SOP-OPS-002 sampling
sources.quote: Take a wellhead sample within 1 hour of a High-High alarm, using the dedicated sand sampling point and a fine mesh sand catcher or centrifuge tube.

sources.label: SOP-OPS-002 responsibilities
sources.quote: **Production Engineer:** sets and reviews sand-free drawdown limits, approves the return to normal rate.
